title: The ponds
hookLine: locals said Walden had no bottom; he sounded it in winter and found it deep but not bottomless (Walden 16)

cards: Winter on Walden Pond. The ice is thick enough to walk on, and a man is out in the middle with an axe, a compass, a measuring chain, and a long line with a stone tied to the end.

He cuts a hole, drops the stone, and waits for the line to go slack. Then he writes something down, walks on, and cuts another hole. Around town there were stories that this pond had no bottom at all.
Thoreau had a simpler idea. Go and find out.

teach.b: First, the story. In The Pond in Winter, Thoreau tells us people said Walden had no bottom.

He's dry about it: "It is remarkable how long men will believe in the bottomlessness of a pond without taking the trouble to sound it." The story had lasted because nobody had checked. Second, the checking.
Thoreau was a working surveyor, and he did the plain thing a surveyor does.

In winter, standing on the ice, with compass and chain and sounding line, he measured the pond. Walden is deep, he found, unusually deep, but the line always came back with a floor under it. Deep, not bottomless.
Third, the turn. You might expect him to laugh at the old story and move on. He doesn't.
He writes, "While men believe in the infinite some ponds will be thought to be bottomless." He understands the wish: people want something in their lives that goes down forever.
He just won't let a pond be the thing that carries it falsely. Fourth, the use of it. Some worries feel like Walden in the old stories.
You look in, and there's no floor, just dark going down. Often nobody has dropped a line. Thoreau's lesson isn't that the worry is shallow; the pond was truly deep.
It's that deep and bottomless are different words, and the way to find out which one you have is to go out on the ice and measure.

how: Readers often take Thoreau's sounding of Walden as a model for meeting fears and rumors: honoring how deep something is, while checking whether it really has no bottom.

o: Walden's water, sounded through ice: deep, with a floor

games.q: inside the ponds: tap the pairs.

s: Thoreau found that Walden really had no bottom
he sounded it through the ice and found it deep, but with a bottom.
Thoreau measured the pond in winter, standing on the ice
with compass, chain and sounding line, he says, before the ice broke up.
Thoreau mocked anyone who longed for something bottomless
he wrote that while people believe in the infinite, some ponds will be thought bottomless.

games.q: everyone in town says the pond has no bottom. you're a surveyor, and it's winter. what do you do?
o: believe the story. everyone says so.
laugh at it and never think about it again.
walk out on the ice and drop a line.
games.why: Thoreau sounded the pond and found it deep but not bottomless, and still treated the old wish for the infinite with respect.

practice: Let one worry come up, not the heaviest, just a real one, and drop a line: what do you actually know about it for sure, and what's the likely outcome, not the wildest one?
If the hard thing happened, what would still be under you: a person, a skill, a next step? You don't have to make it small; just find where the floor is, then breathe out and let the line rest.

wordCard.voice: The ponds. Thoreau sounded Walden through the winter ice and found it deep, but with a bottom. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: deep, not bottomless. A real depth still has a floor somewhere under it. Until tomorrow.
